## Let's try an example

Run this code on your computer

```{r echo = TRUE}
s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
mean(s)
```

## Let's try an example

If there were thousands of us, the result would look more and more perfectly [normal]{.alert}

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
foo <- replicate(10000, {
    s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
    mean(s)
})

dat <- data.frame(Sample_Mean = foo)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Sample_Mean)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                   bins = 20) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = mean(dat$Sample_Mean),
                              sd = sd(dat$Sample_Mean)))
```

## Let's try an example

In case you are curious, here is the code for making that graphic

```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
foo <- replicate(10000, {
    s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
    mean(s)
})

dat <- data.frame(Sample_Mean = foo)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Sample_Mean)) +

```

## The normal distribution allows many useful methods

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
set.seed(1)
noni_dat <- data.frame(sed = c(rnorm(100, -2), rnorm(100)),
                       group = c(rep("10mg noni", 100),
                                 rep("placebo", 100)))

set.seed(2)
fish_data <- data.frame(pollution = runif(100, 0, 100))
fish_data$body <- rnorm(100, 20 - 0.1 * fish_data$pollution, 2)
fish_data$impact <- cut(fish_data$pollution, c(0, 33, 66, 100),
                        labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

p1 <- ggplot(noni_dat, aes(x = sed, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(group)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("Change in sed rate [mm/hr]\n(after - before)") +
    ggtitle("Comparison of Means")

p2 <- ggplot(fish_data, aes(x = impact, y = body)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Level of human impact") +
    ylab("Reef fish biomass (g)")

p3 <- ggplot(fish_data, aes(x = pollution, y = body)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Pollution (ppm)") +
    ylab("Reef fish biomass (g)")

p23 <- plot_grid(p2, p3, labels = c("Analysis of Variance",
                                    "Correlation and Regression"),
                 ncol = 1)
plot_grid(p1, p23, ncol = 2)
```

## Learning Objectives

1. *Describe the properties of a normal distribution*
2. *Know that the standard error of the sampling distribution of size $n$ from the normal distribution equals* $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$
3. *Find the probability density of a range of sample mean*
4. *Use a Z-transform to convert any normal distribution into the standard normal distribution*
6. *Explain why normal distributions are common, and explain the Central Limit Theorem*
6. Use *R* to make calculations about and sample from a normal distribution
5. Interpret histograms and qq-plots to meaningfully evaluate if data are roughly normal
7. Transform non-normal data to become normal

## [Normal distribution]{.alert}

> The [normal distribution]{.alert} is a continuous probability distribution describing a bell-shaped curve. It is a good approximation to the frequency distribution of many biological variables.

## The [normal distribution]{.alert} has two parameters, mean and standard deviation

For the population, consider a continuous variable $Y$ with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$

$$f(Y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e ^ {\frac{-(Y - \mu) ^ 2}{2 \sigma ^ 2}}$$
$f(Y)$ is the probability density associated with a value $Y$

Higher probability when:

1. $Y$ is close to $\mu$

2. The spread of the distribution is low ($\sigma$ is small)

## The [normal distribution]{.alert} has two parameters, mean and standard deviation

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="80%"}
x <- read.csv("../data/bird_morpho.csv")

df1 <- x[x$species %in% c("jawe", "rwbu", "wrsh"), ] |>
    group_by(full_name) |>
    summarize(
        n = n(),
        mu = mean(nares_to_tip, na.rm = TRUE),
        sigma = sd(nares_to_tip, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    mutate(label = glue("mean = {mu}, sd = {sigma}",
                        mu = round(mu, 1),
                        sigma = round(sigma, 2)))

df2 <- df1 |>
    crossing(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01)) |>
    mutate(x1 = mu + x * sigma, y = dnorm(x1, mu, sigma))

ggplot(x[x$species %in% c("jawe", "rwbu", "wrsh"), ],
       aes(fill = full_name)) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(full_name),
               labeller = labeller(full_name = label_wrap_gen(width = 10))) +
    geom_histogram(mapping = aes(nares_to_tip, y = ..density..),
                   show.legend = FALSE, binwidth = 0.2) +
    geom_line(data = df2, mapping = aes(x1, y), size = 2, color = "darkgrey") +
    geom_text(data = df1, mapping = aes(x = 5, y = 1, label = label), hjust = 0,
              size = 8) +
    xlab("Beak length (mm)") +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 20)
    )
```

## Properties of a [normal distribution]{.alert}

* Continuous distribution
* Symmetrical around its mean
* It has a single mode
* The probability density is highest exactly at the mean

## Discrete versus Continuous distributions

```{r, fig.align='center', out.width="80%"}
df1 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, 1), y = dbinom(x, size = 10, prob = 0.5))
df2 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

gp1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(fill = "tomato") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
  xlab("Number of success") +
  ylab("Probability") +
  ggtitle("Binomial (discrete)") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

gp2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle("Normal (continuous)") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

plot_grid(gp1, gp2)
```

## Discrete versus Continuous distributions

Discrete: Probability of 5 successes is `r round(dbinom(5, 10, 0.5), 2)`

Continuous: Probability of $`r round(qnorm(0.375), 2)` < Y < `r round(qnorm(0.625), 2)`$ is 0.25

```{r, fig.align='center', out.width="80%"}
gp3 <- gp1 +
  geom_col(
    data = filter(df1, x == 5),
    fill = "steelblue"
  )

gp4 <- gp2 +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(df2, x > qnorm(0.375), x < qnorm(0.625)),
    fill = "steelblue"
  )

plot_grid(gp3, gp4)
```

## Symmetrical around its mean

```{r, fig.align='center', out.width="80%"}
df1 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 20, 0.01), y = dchisq(x, df = 6))
df2 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

gp1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(chi^2)) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle(expression(bold(paste(chi[6]^2, " (asymmetrical)")))) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

gp2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle("Normal (symmetrical)") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

plot_grid(gp1, gp2)
```

## Symmetrical around its mean

Asymmetric: Probability of $\chi^2 > \text{mean}$ is `r round(pchisq(6, 6, lower.tail = FALSE), 2)`

Symmetric: Probability of $Y > \text{mean}$ is `r round(pnorm(0, lower.tail = FALSE), 2)`

```{r, fig.align='center', out.width="80%"}
gp3 <- gp1 +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(df1, x > 6),
    fill = "steelblue"
  )

gp4 <- gp2 +
  geom_area(
    data = filter(df2, x > 0),
    fill = "steelblue"
  )

plot_grid(gp3, gp4)
```

## The probability density is highest exactly at the mean

```{r, fig.align='center', out.width="80%"}
df1 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 20, 0.01), y = dchisq(x, df = 6))
df2 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

gp1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6, size = 3, linetype = "dashed") +
  xlab(expression(chi^2)) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle(expression(bold(paste(chi[6]^2, " (highest density < mean)")))) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

gp2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, size = 3, linetype = "dashed") +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle("Normal (highest density = mean)") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

plot_grid(gp1, gp2)
```

## Properties of a [normal distribution]{.alert}

* Continuous distribution
* Symmetrical around its mean
* It has a single mode
* The probability density is highest exactly at the mean

## Standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma_{\overline{Y}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$

The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution

If we take a sample of $n$ from a normally distributed population with standard deviation $\sigma$, the population standard error of the sample mean is:

$$\sigma_{\overline{Y}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$$

## Standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma_{\overline{Y}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$

::: {.pause-think}
If $\sigma = 1$, which panels show the sampling distribution of the sample mean associated with $n = 4$, $n = 9$, and $n = 25$?
:::

```{r, fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=2}
se <- c(A = 1/5, B = 1/2, C = 1/3)
df <- crossing(x = seq(-2, 2, 0.1), g = names(se)) |>
    mutate(x1 = x, "Probability density" = dnorm(x1, 0, se))

gp <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x1, y = `Probability density`)) +
    geom_line() +
    xlab(expression(italic(bar(Y)))) +
    theme_cowplot()

gp + facet_grid(cols = vars(g))
```

## Standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma_{\overline{Y}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$

::: {.pause-think}
If $\sigma = 1$

| $n$ | standard error of the sample mean |
|:--:|:--:|
| 4  | $1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2$ |
| 9  | $1/\sqrt{9} = 1/3$ |
| 25 | $1/\sqrt{25} = 1/5$ |
:::

```{r, fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=2, out.height="45%"}
gp + facet_grid(cols = vars(g),
                labeller = as_labeller(c(A = "n = 25",
                                         B = "n = 4",
                                         C = "n = 9")))
```

## The probability density of a sample mean

If $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the probability of the sample mean $\overline{Y} = 1.0$ for $n = 4$?

Trick question: with a continuous variable, the probability of any exact value of $\overline{Y}$ is infinitesimal ($\approx 0$).

## The probability density of a sample mean

If $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the probability **density** of the sample mean $\overline{Y} = 1.0$ for $n = 4$?

We can answer this!

In *R*

```{r, echo = TRUE}
dnorm(1.0, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(4))
```

This does **NOT** mean there is a 10% chance of $\overline{Y} = 1.0$

## The probability density of a range of sample means

If $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the probability **density** that the sample mean $\overline{Y} \ge 1.0$ for $n = 4$?

Trick question: probability density is associated with a specific value of $\overline{Y}$.

## The probability of a range of sample means

If $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the probability that the sample mean $\overline{Y} \ge 1.0$ for $n = 4$?

We can answer this!

In *R*

```{r, echo = TRUE}
pnorm(1.0, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(4), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

This means there is a 2.28% chance of $\overline{Y} \ge 1.0$

## The probability of a range of sample means

The probability density $f(Y)$ associated with $\overline{Y}$ is the height of the curve

The probability of a range of sample means in the area under the curve for that range

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="70%"}
df <- tibble(
  x = seq(-2, 2, 0.01),
  y = dnorm(x, 0, 0.5)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, x >= 1), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_line(size = 2) +
  xlim(-2, 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(bar(Y)))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
  )
```

## All normal distributions can be described by $\mu$ and $\sigma$

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="85%"}
df <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(size = 2, fill = "tomato", color = "black") +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-2, 2, 1), labels = c(expression(mu - 2 * sigma), expression(mu - sigma), expression(mu), expression(mu + sigma), expression(mu + 2 * sigma))) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
  )
```

## The [standard normal distribution]{.alert} has $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="85%"}
df <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(size = 2, fill = "tomato", color = "black") +
  xlab(expression(italic(Z))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-2, 2, 1)) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
  )
```

## The [standard normal distribution]{.alert} has $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$

$Z$-transformation: transform any normal distribution to a standard normal

$$Z = \frac{Y - \mu}{\sigma}$$

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$\mu = 1$, $\sigma = 2$

| $Y$ | $Z$ |
|:--:|:--:|
| -1 | $\frac{-1 - 1}{2} = -1$ |
| 1  | $\frac{1 - 1}{2} = 0$ |
| 3  | $\frac{3 - 1}{2} = 1$ |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$\mu = -2$, $\sigma = 3$

| $Y$ | $Z$ |
|:--:|:--:|
| -5 | $\frac{-5 - (-2)}{3} = -1$ |
| -2 | $\frac{-2 - (-2)}{3} = 0$ |
| 1  | $\frac{1 - (-2)}{3} = 1$ |
:::
:::

## $Z$: [standard normal deviate]{.alert}

> A [standard normal deviate]{.alert}, or $Z$, tells us how many standard deviations a particular value is from the mean

## [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert}

> According to the [central limit theorem]{.alert}, the sum or mean of a large number of measurements randomly sampled from a non-normal population is approximately normally distributed.

## Why the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert} matters

1. It explains why so many quantities are normally distributed
2. When $n$ is large, many statistical tests that assume data are normal sampling distributions work OK
3. It can speed up calculations for large samples from non-normal distributions

## Because of the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert}...

**the world is shockingly normal**

Run this code on your computer

```{r echo = TRUE,  eval = FALSE}
s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
mean(s)
```

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
                   bins = 20) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = mean(dat$Sample_Mean),
                              sd = sd(dat$Sample_Mean)))
```

## [Normal distribution]{.alert}

> The [normal distribution]{.alert} is a continuous probability distribution describing a bell-shaped curve. It is a good approximation to the frequency distribution of many biological variables.

## The [normal distribution]{.alert} has two parameters, mean and standard deviation

For the population, consider a continuous variable $Y$ with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$

$$f(Y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e ^ {\frac{-(Y - \mu) ^ 2}{2 \sigma ^ 2}}$$
$f(Y)$ is the probability density associated with a value $Y$

Higher probability when:

1. $Y$ is close to $\mu$

2. The spread of the distribution is low ($\sigma$ is small)

## The [normal distribution]{.alert} has two parameters, mean and standard deviation

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="80%"}
x <- read.csv("../data/bird_morpho.csv")

df1 <- x[x$species %in% c("jawe", "rwbu", "wrsh"), ] |>
    group_by(full_name) |>
    summarize(
        n = n(),
        mu = mean(nares_to_tip, na.rm = TRUE),
        sigma = sd(nares_to_tip, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    mutate(label = glue("mean = {mu}, sd = {sigma}",
                        mu = round(mu, 1),
                        sigma = round(sigma, 2)))

df2 <- df1 |>
    crossing(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01)) |>
    mutate(x1 = mu + x * sigma, y = dnorm(x1, mu, sigma))

ggplot(x[x$species %in% c("jawe", "rwbu", "wrsh"), ],
       aes(fill = full_name)) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(full_name),
               labeller = labeller(full_name = label_wrap_gen(width = 10))) +
    geom_histogram(mapping = aes(nares_to_tip, y = ..density..),
                   show.legend = FALSE, binwidth = 0.2) +
    geom_line(data = df2, mapping = aes(x1, y), size = 2, color = "darkgrey") +
    geom_text(data = df1, mapping = aes(x = 5, y = 1, label = label), hjust = 0,
              size = 8) +
    xlab("Beak length (mm)") +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    scale_fill_viridis_d() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 20)
    )
```

## [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert}

> According to the [central limit theorem]{.alert}, the sum or mean of a large number of measurements randomly sampled from a non-normal population is approximately normally distributed.

## Why the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert} matters

1. It explains why so many quantities are normally distributed
2. When $n$ is large, many statistical tests that assume data are normal sampling distributions work OK
3. It can speed up calculations for large samples from non-normal distributions

## Because of the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert}...

**the world is shockingly normal**

Run this code on your computer

```{r echo = TRUE,  eval = FALSE}
s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
mean(s)
```

## Because of the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert}...

**the world is shockingly normal**

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
foo <- replicate(5000, {
    s <- sample(20, 5, replace = TRUE)
    mean(s)
})

dat <- data.frame(Sample_Mean = foo)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Sample_Mean)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y =..density..),
                   bins = 20) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = mean(dat$Sample_Mean),
                              sd = sd(dat$Sample_Mean)))
```

## Use R to calculate densities, probabilities, and quantiles from normal distributions

Given a normal distribution with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the probability **density** of the value 1?

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=3, fig.height=3, out.width="80%"}
x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, 0.01)
df1 <- data.frame(x = x, y = dnorm(x))

ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
    xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 1, y = 0, xend = 1, yend = dnorm(1),
                     color = "tomato"),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.03, "npc"))) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 1, y = dnorm(1), xend = -1.05 * 3.5, yend = dnorm(1),
                     color = "tomato"),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.03, "npc"))) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = 1.05 * c(-3.5, 3.5), expand = c(0, 0))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r, echo = TRUE}
dnorm(1.0, mean = 0, sd = 1)
```
:::
:::

## Use R to calculate densities, probabilities, and quantiles from normal distributions

Given a normal distribution with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, what's the 10% quantile?

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=3, fig.height=3, out.width="80%"}
q10 <- qnorm(0.1)

ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, fill="gray",
              xlim = c(-3.5, q10)) +
    geom_line(color = "black", size = 2) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = q10, y = dnorm(q10),
                     xend = q10, yend = -0.05 * dnorm(0),
                     color = "tomato"),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.03, "npc"))) +
    xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = 1.05 * c(-3.5, 3.5), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.05 * dnorm(0), 1.05 * dnorm(0)),
                       expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Quantile-quantile plot

A useful visual tool for assessing normality in a sample

## QQ plot examples

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="80%"}
set.seed(20210325)
df1 <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, 0.01), y = dnorm(x))
df2 <- tibble(Y = rnorm(1e3))
df3 <- tibble(x = seq(0, 6, 0.01), y = dlnorm(x))
df4 <- tibble(Y = rlnorm(1e3))

gp1 <- ggplot(df1, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(color = "black", fill = "tomato", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle("Normal distribution") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(sample = Y)) +
  geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
  geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  ggtitle("Normal QQ Plot") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp3 <- ggplot(df3, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(color = "black", fill = "tomato", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  ggtitle("Right-skewed distribution") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp4 <- ggplot(df4, aes(sample = Y)) +
  geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
  geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  ggtitle("Right-skewed QQ Plot") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

plot_grid(gp1, gp2, gp3, gp4, nrow = 2)
```

## Log-transformation is very useful for right-skewed distributions

There are many transformations

Log-transformation is by the far the most useful in biology

Other situations (left-skew, long tails, bimodality) involve more complex approaches

## Log-transformation is very useful for right-skewed distributions

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="80%"}
set.seed(20210325)
df4 <- tibble(Y = rlnorm(1e3))

gp1 <- ggplot(df4, aes(Y)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "tomato", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(Y))) +
  ggtitle("Right-skewed sample") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp2 <- ggplot(df4, aes(sample = Y)) +
  geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
  geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  ggtitle("Right-skewed QQ Plot") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp3 <- ggplot(df4, aes(log(Y))) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "tomato", size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(log(italic(Y)))) +
  ggtitle("After log-transformation") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

gp4 <- ggplot(df4, aes(sample = log(Y))) +
  geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
  geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  ggtitle("After log-transformation") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

plot_grid(gp1, gp2, gp3, gp4, nrow = 2)
```

## Log-transformation is very useful for right-skewed distributions

**How do you log-transform your data?**

```{r echo = TRUE}
# read-in one of our example datasets: mammal masses
mam <- read.csv("../data/mammals.csv")

# add a log-transformed body mass column
mam$log_body_mass <- log(mam$body_mass_kg)
```

## Log-transformation is very useful for right-skewed distributions

**How do you log-transform your data?**

This is how you display a qq-plot

```{r echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
ggplot(mam, aes(sample = log_body_mass)) +
    geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
    geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Theoretical quantiles") +
    ylab("Observed quantiles")
```

```{r fig.align="center", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, out.height="70%"}

    geom_histogram(fill = "tomato", bins = 20) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    ggtitle("Log-transformed")

histlin <- ggplot(mam, aes(x = body_mass_kg)) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "tomato", bins = 20) +
    theme_cowplot()+

qqlog <- ggplot(mam, aes(sample = log_body_mass)) +
    geom_qq(color = "tomato") +
    geom_qq_line(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab("Theoretical quantiles") +

qqlin <- ggplot(mam, aes(sample = body_mass_kg)) +

plot_grid(histlin, histlog, qqlin, qqlog, nrow = 2)
```
